young.html: Prince Hamlet of Denmark comes home from university because his father, the King, has died. Worse, his uncle Claudius has become king and married Hamlet's mother, all in a few weeks. Hamlet is heartbroken.

Then, on the castle walls at midnight, a ghost appears: it looks like his father. It tells Hamlet that Claudius murdered him, and asks Hamlet to set things right. But is the ghost telling the truth? Hamlet decides to find out. He pretends to be a little mad, and he has some traveling actors put on a play that shows a murder like his father's, while he watches his uncle's face.

young.html: Hamlet is famous because he thinks so hard about everything: about whether to act, about life and death, about what people are. His speeches have become some of the most quoted words in English.

For parents: Hamlet is a revenge tragedy, and most of the main characters die by the end. Young readers can follow Acts I and II (the ghost, the madness and the actors) and a good retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

Test the ghost. Hamlet cannot be sure the ghost is honest, so he sets a test. If you had to find out whether someone was telling the truth, without asking them, what test would you design? Is it fair to test people that way?
young.title: Talk it over

full.html: Hamlet (c. 1600) is Shakespeare's longest play and probably his most discussed. He took the old story of a Danish prince's revenge, known from a Danish chronicle of about 1200 and an earlier English play now lost, and turned it into a play about thinking, doubt and grief. It survives in three early versions (printed 1603, 1604 and 1623), which differ.

full.text:
The time is out of joint. O cursed spite,
That ever I was born to set it right.
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.note: "Out of joint" means dislocated, like a shoulder. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: Hamlet promises revenge at the end of Act I and does not achieve it until the last scene. Why? He is not sure the Ghost is honest; it might be a devil in his father's shape. He blames himself for thinking too much. He spares Claudius at prayer for fear of sending his soul to heaven. Each explanation fits some scenes, and readers have argued for four hundred years.

full.text: To be, or not to be

To be, or not to be, that is the question:
Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer
The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,
Or to take arms against a sea of troubles,
And by opposing end them?
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: In this soliloquy (a speech alone, thinking aloud) Hamlet weighs whether life's suffering is worth bearing, and concludes that fear of what may come after death keeps people going, and that too much thinking makes us slow to act. It is a speech about a question, not a decision.

full.text: What a piece of work is man, how noble in reason, how infinite in faculties, in form and moving, how express and admirable; in action how like an angel, in apprehension, how like a god: the beauty of the world, the paragon of animals.
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.note: Hamlet speaks this in prose. He goes on to say that man delights him not. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: The speech sums up the Renaissance praise of human greatness, and Hamlet, in his grief, can no longer feel it. That gap between what he knows and what he feels is the heart of the play.

Hamlet kills Polonius by mistake, is sent away, escapes, and returns calmer, ready to let things come. A fencing match with Laertes, rigged by Claudius with a poisoned blade and a poisoned cup, ends with the deaths of the Queen, Laertes, Claudius and Hamlet. Hamlet asks Horatio to live and tell his story, and the Norwegian prince Fortinbras takes the crown.

Thinking Hamlet is simply weak or indecisive. He acts boldly at times (the play, the escape at sea). The play asks harder questions: how to act rightly when you cannot be sure, and whether revenge can ever set the world right.

deep.html: Hamlet, Laertes and Fortinbras have all lost fathers. Laertes rushes to revenge and is used by Claudius; Fortinbras acts without a second thought; Hamlet thinks. Shakespeare sets them side by side and lets us compare.

items: Can we ever be certain enough to act? What should we do when we are not?
Is revenge justice, or does it only make more wrongs?
Is Hamlet's madness real, pretended, or both?
What does Hamlet learn by the end, when he says "the readiness is all"?

deep.html: Montaigne's Essays, on this ladder, share Hamlet's habit of doubt, and many scholars think Shakespeare read them. Sophocles' Oedipus, earlier, is another tragedy of a man who must discover a hidden crime.

questions: Hamlet cannot be sure the ghost is telling the truth. What should you do when you cannot be sure?
Is it better to think carefully before acting, or to act quickly? When is each one right?
Polonius says "to thine own self be true." What does that mean to you?
Hamlet asks Horatio to tell his story. Why does it matter to him that someone tells it truly?
care: Hamlet is a revenge tragedy: it includes murder, grief, Ophelia's drowning and the deaths of most of the main characters. This lesson summarizes these without detail and quotes nothing violent.
